title: Voters in 2 North Dakota counties reject property tax increases
description: Voters in two North Dakota counties Tuesday defeated ballot measures to raise property taxes beyond a 3% cap set by the Legislature last year.  The measures came as an early sign of how some counties have grappled to cover rising costs under the limitation set by the Legislature last year. Divide County asked voters to […]
text:
The Traill County Courthouse in Hillsboro, North Dakota. (Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)Voters in two North Dakota counties Tuesday defeated ballot measures to raise property taxes beyond a 3% cap set by the Legislature last year. 
The measures came as an early sign of how some counties have grappled to cover rising costs under the limitation set by the Legislature last year.
Divide County asked voters to approve an additional 2%, or about $37,800 per year over the next four years to help fund the county’s operations. Voters said “no” by a 53% majority, according to complete but unofficial results. Divide turnout was nearly 58%, well above the barely 40% statewide. 
In Traill County, officials put on a measure of an additional 6.41%, or about $461,000 per year over the next four years, to help fund various services due to increasing costs and hiring competition with nearby Fargo and Grand Forks. Voters shot it down by more than 61%. Traill turnout was about 50%, also above the statewide number.
Additionally, seven county measures for increased mill levies failed around the state; only one passed, said Donnell Preskey, government/public relations specialist for the North Dakota Association of Counties. 
“The economy is a big concern, and I think people are just not wanting any more expenses,” she said.
2 North Dakota counties ask voters to override property tax cap

Divide and Traill county officials previously told the North Dakota Monitor that they would have to make budget cuts if voters rejected the measures. Potential examples include full-time positions moved to part-time, delayed road projects and no salary increases.
For such measures to pass, citizens need to better understand the need for more revenue, Preskey said. Counties will have to prioritize and cut certain things due to their limited revenue, she said.
The 2025 Legislature set the 3% cap on annual property tax increases by local governments as part of an expansion of a primary residence property tax credit. The legislation came months after a 2024 ballot initiative that sought to eliminate assessed-value property taxes and force the state to pick up the tab for billions of dollars in replacement revenue. Voters rejected that measure. 
Many counties have used reserves and/or all or part of the 3% property tax increase allowed by law for their 2026 budget, according to data Preskey presented to lawmakers this year.
The Association of Counties supports exceptions to the 3% cap for counties’ difficult costs of health insurance, elections and jails.
House Finance and Taxation Committee Chairman Craig Headland, R-Montpelier, has said he senses no appetite to increase or eliminate the 3% cap.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Pillen eyes 2028 ballot if Nebraska lawmakers again stall on property tax reform
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen hasn’t budged on his approach to cap local spending and cover K-12 education costs to alleviate property taxes he’s called for in the past four years. But in 2027, Pillen’s second term begins with a more skeptical, divided Legislature to his ideas than before. Though he is adding a backstop: […]
text:
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen hosts a news conference talking about his approach for property taxes ahead of the 2027 legislative session on Nov. 6, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska, days after securing reelection for four more years. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen hasn’t budged on his approach to cap local spending and cover K-12 education costs to alleviate property taxes he’s called for in the past four years.
But in 2027, Pillen’s second term begins with a more skeptical, divided Legislature to his ideas than before. Though he is adding a backstop: If the Legislature fails, he’ll go to the 2028 ballot.
“All of us, from the river to Harrison, from Falls City to Chadron, from South Sioux City to Benkelman, we’re all ticked off. It’s got to be fixed,” Pillen said at a 30-minute news conference.
Gov. Jim Pillen is joined by two dozen lawmakers for a news conference at the end of the Legislature’s special session to address property taxes that began almost one month prior. Aug. 20, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Many of Pillen’s proposals are familiar — capping local property taxes and valuations, having the state take on the operational costs of K-12 schools and encouraging local governments to cut spending to lower property taxes. The governor said Nebraskans “spoke loud and clear” and gave him and other state leaders a “mandate” to “solve the property tax crisis.” 
He said his ideas should receive bipartisan legislative support and that a broadened sales tax base remains a solution, which is “such a no-brainer, it’s unbelievable, such common sense.”
“I believe in it so much that if we don’t get things accomplished in ‘27, our team will be working on taking it to the ballot for ‘28, and we’ll let the people speak,” Pillen said.
Going to the 2028 ballot
As for what going to the 2028 ballot would look like if needed — petitions, a legislative constitutional amendment (which requires 30 votes) or wading into legislative races — Pillen said he could not say. Some Republican lawmakers are proactively raising funds for reelection should they face primary challengers for opposing Pillen’s ideas.
“I don’t have all those specifics worked out in our head, but all I’m telling you is that we’re dead serious about fighting for Nebraskans to solve this property tax crisis,” Pillen said.
Data that Gov. Jim Pillen’s team compiled showing how state property tax relief has affected effective property tax collections over time is projected during a news conference Nov. 6, 2026, in the Nebraska State Capitol in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The governor also could not say exactly what deadline he’s imposing, such as whether it’s early on in the 2027 session, when the session ends in late May or a special session in the summer
Said Pillen, “We’ll just see what the attitude of the new Legislature is.”
“If the Legislature doesn’t want to solve the problem, we’ll get started sooner than later,” Pillen continued. “If they’re open to the conversation, if they’re going to make it a red-blue conversation, we’ll figure that out pretty quickly. It doesn’t take a rocket scientist to know that.”
The governor presented data his team compiled indicating that ongoing property tax relief efforts, including state credits to offset local costs, have turned the tide on property taxes. For property taxes on agricultural land, for instance, Pillen said collections are effectively the same as 2013 levels. For residential property, it’s back to 2021 levels, and for commercial property, taxpayers are paying what they did in 2019.
Eric Underwood of Lincoln, former chair of the Nebraska Republican Party, has outlined a 15-petition effort aimed at the 2028 election, including many on property taxes. 
It’s not yet clear whether Pillen might lend support to Underwood’s proposals.
A changing Legislature
Multiple lawmakers who usually supported Pillen’s ideas, such as broadening sales tax revenue, include term-limited state Sens. Rob Clements of Elmwood, Speaker John Arch of La Vista and Ben Hansen of Blair. Those three Republicans will be succeeded by more skeptical conservatives who have expressed some concern about a tax “shift” or more taxation.
The 2026 candidates for the Nebraska Legislature arranged by district. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The Legislature’s 33-Republican legislative supermajority — the minimum votes needed to overcome a filibuster — is also set to end. State Sen. Merv Riepe of Ralston, a Republican, lost reelection, and two other Omaha-area races could flip blue or purple. State Sen. Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn, Revenue Committee chair, is another Republican who could lose reelection if results hold. He was seen as a frontrunner to succeed Arch as speaker.
Pillen has called for lowering the threshold to end filibusters from 33 to 30. However, a majority of lawmakers, across geography and ideology, have said they’re opposed to the idea.
As he’s done in the past, Pillen said his solution is talking more with lawmakers. He said he and his team will “communicate nonstop.”
“When we can all agree on what a definition of a tax shift is, what the definition of a tax cut is, it starts becoming crystal clear that we’ve been duped by special-interest lobbying groups for 50 years,” Pillen said.
He views sales taxes as the right solution because taxpayers can choose whether to make those purchases, as opposed to mandatory income or property taxes. He noted laundry services and ironing of clothes, for instance, which he said he’s done a few times. He joked that first lady Suzanne Pillen might argue with his ironing a little bit.
“I’ll iron my shirt. I’ll mow my own lawn. I’ll wash my car. I’ll do all the normal things that we used to do,” Pillen said. “That’s not people that are in tough shape. They have that opportunity.”
Yet for multiple years, Pillen has tried to rally lawmakers behind his cause. The needle hasn’t moved to push it over the edge of narrow defeats multiple times over.
2026 special session?
Multiple returning lawmakers and lobbyists have questioned whether Pillen might pursue a special session in the next two months, possibly with a more favorable Legislature. Some have wondered whether Pillen might try to cut spending, and some lawmakers have speculated whether legislators could pause lowering income tax rates before it lowers to 3.99% in January.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen hosts a news conference talking about his approach for property taxes ahead of the 2027 legislative session on Nov. 6, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska, days after securing reelection for four more years. At right is a map the governor said shows the “mandate” he and other state leaders have to act based on unofficial election results and margins between Republicans and Democrats. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“Anything could be possible” in a special session, Pillen said, though he said he has not talked to any lawmakers as he’s “worked my brains out” running the state and running for reelection.
“I gave up speculation a long time ago because it almost broke me trying to speculate markets,” Pillen said.
Pillen called a special session in the summer of 2024 solely on property taxes.
However, multiple state senators and lobbyists the Nebraska Examiner has spoken to for months have said few ideas might have 33 votes to pass in 2026, let alone before a new Legislature with more than a dozen fresh faces coming in at voters’ wishes on Jan. 6.
Balancing Nebraska’s budget
Largely absent from Friday’s news conference was talk about Nebraska’s budget, likely in part because Pillen denies that Nebraska is in a “budget crisis.” Some Republicans, such as former state Sen. Julie Slama of Dunbar, have broken from Pillen and called it a “crisis.”
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen talks with reporters after declaring victory in his reelection bid to lead the Cornhusker State on Nov. 4, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Through mid-2029, Nebraska faces a budget deficit that could grow as high as $1.2 billion.
“Those numbers over three years are not near as complicated,” Pillen told reporters.
Pillen said he held a cabinet meeting Friday and spent a couple of minutes celebrating cultural improvements and the work that’s already been done. He said the expectation across the Executive Branch is that agency heads will be in the office, rolling up their sleeves and finding efficiencies, such as cutting out “silly things” happening in government.
“Really, really crystal clear: Pleased but sure as heck not satisfied,” Pillen said of his cabinet.
The Legislature convenes Jan. 6. Pillen’s next four-year term begins the next day.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC’s new constitutional amendments pose financial dilemmas for state, local lawmakers
description: North Carolina voters who delivered a blue wave for Democrats Tuesday also overwhelmingly approved two constitutional amendments that will impact taxes for years to come. The first amendment, approved by 62% of voters, caps state income tax rates for individuals and corporations at 3.5%. The second amendment, which 60% of voters approved, requires the state [...]
text:
North Carolina voters overwhelmingly passed three constitutional amendments on Nov. 3, 2026 to authorize lawmakers to impose limits on local governments’ power to raise property taxes, cap the state income tax, and require photo ID for all voters — not just those voting in person. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) North Carolina voters who delivered a blue wave for Democrats Tuesday also overwhelmingly approved two constitutional amendments that will impact taxes for years to come.
The first amendment, approved by 62% of voters, caps state income tax rates for individuals and corporations at 3.5%. The second amendment, which 60% of voters approved, requires the state legislature to limit increases in local property taxes, reducing the money communities can raise for schools, infrastructure and other needs.
Alexandra Sirota (Photo: NC Budget & Tax Center)
Alexandra Sirota, director of the North Carolina Budget & Tax Center, said Wednesday that the outcome of the constitutional amendments was deeply disappointing for the future of the state.
“We know that people were voting out of concern for rising costs, and we know that one of the best ways for our state leaders to address those rising costs is to fund programs and services that make life more affordable,” said Sirota. “Unfortunately, the tax amendments that passed put in place real limits on future policymakers’ ability to adjust their revenue to the needs of the moment.”
Sirota said the amendments don’t alter the need for increased investments in childcare, housing, and transportation infrastructure. The property tax measure also doesn’t offer any specifics about how the limit should work.
“It really is going to be up to state legislators to craft the exact language and the exact limit that they want to place on local governments,” Sirota said.
 Amendments could hamstring local governments 
Sirota said the proposed property tax limit could affect communities’ ability to upgrade infrastructure through future bonds, fill the gap when the federal government cuts food assistance, or put more money into public education.
This week the State Board of Education released a new report that detailed $18 billion in school facility needs over the next five years for the state’s 115 school systems.
Local governments often use property taxes to fund school capital projects. The newly passed constitutional amendment could limit that.
“What’s most important in this policy development is going to be having the time to really carefully consider how this gets implemented so that local governments are able to keep up with the rising costs they’re being asked to take on,” said Sirota.
New leadership, new ideas 
Rep. Deb Butler, D-New Hanover, said there’s no doubt that the amendments will present new challenges for legislators who now have to decide  how to structure limits on local property taxes without adversely affecting local government services.
Rep. Deb Butler, D-New Hanover (Photo: NCGA)
“Those are going to be some constraints that we’re going to have to work within,” Butler told NC Newsline.
Butler is a senior member of the House Finance Committee who has expressed interest in taking the reins of the committee when Democrats take control of the House in January.
“That’s of course the decision of the Speaker,” said Butler. “But I’ve been working on some ideas about how we generate more revenue, how we get rid of some of these ‘favorite son’ exemptions and how we level the playing field with corporations.”
Butler said the key will be to find a way to create new revenue for North Carolina without hurting small businesses or individual taxpayers.
 Limiting state revenue growth 
Under the state income tax amendment voters approved, the state’s maximum income tax rate is 3.5%. North Carolina’s personal income tax rate currently stands at 3.99%. It’s slated to fall to 3.49% in January, and fall again to 3.24% in 2030 .
North Carolina’s current corporate income tax rate of 2% is scheduled to reach zero by 2030.
The Budget & Tax Center says that as soon as 2028, the state is projected to face real financial challenges if the schedule of rate cuts continues.
“I think the biggest thing that state legislators are going to need to do is stop those scheduled rate cuts to make sure we at least hold the line on funding people’s priorities,” Sirota said.
The State Board of Education released a new report this week that detailed $18 billion in school facility needs over the next five years for the state’s 115 school systems. (Image: Adobe Stock)
In the new school facility needs report, the most common justifications reported for future expenditures are to resolve repairs or deferred maintenance. Plumbing, HVAC, and electrical needs account for $2.8 billion or 30% of all reported renovation needs at the state’s existing schools, according to the Department of Public Instruction.
Sirota notes that the failure to keep up with maintenance needs can often result in greater expense for costly HVAC repairs or mold remediation.
“Those costs need to be met with revenue,” said Sirota.
Sirota said difficult choices lie ahead. She says millionaires are already not being asked to pay their fair share. With the new income tax cap, future lawmakers may need to turn to raising sales taxes or fees, which would be a bigger financial burden on middle- and low-income households.
Some Democrats have suggested repealing the state’s opportunity scholarship program as one source of revenue.
The Republican-controlled legislature earmarked $705 million in its most recent budget for the Opportunity Scholarship Program in 2026-27, with plans to increase that appropriation to over $800 million annually by 2030.
Butler said she’ll leave it up to others in her caucus to determine how to deal with vouchers.
“That is a big source of revenue that needs to be reevaluated,” said Butler.
 Luxuries and loopholes 
Butler said there should be some agreement on easy reforms like removing luxury tax caps in North Carolina.
“In North Carolina, you can buy a $100 million dollar aircraft or yacht, and you pay a tax with a cap of $1,500,” said Butler. “That’s just not right.”
Butler said the next legislature should also revisit the “Blue Ridge exemption,” a property tax loophole for affordable housing that is being used by corporate for-profit developers while costing local governments tens of millions of dollars each year.
Bill to close property tax loophole advances in NC House committee

A bill to close that loophole passed the N.C. House in May, only to languish in the Senate.
“I think there’s a better, fairer way to do that that would generate revenue,” she said.
Butler said as a minority member, she’s had plenty of time to ruminate on some ideas. With a new House Speaker and a new crop of incoming lawmakers, she’s hoping for time to discuss them.
“If I’ve learned anything watching these current leaders, it’s that you don’t do anything in a rushed fashion,” said Butler. “I think about HB2 or the classroom size bill, or any number of things that they’ve gone after at breakneck speed.”
“I’d rather get it right the first time,” Butler said. “These are big changes and you don’t want to do anything that’s going to have unintended consequences.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: North Carolina school facility funding needs climb 37% to nearly $18 billion
description: North Carolina is seeing a steep jump in what it needs to spend on its public school facilities, according to a new report by the state Department of Public Instruction. A newly passed constitutional amendment could make that more difficult.   The 2025–26 statewide facility needs survey, which Vice Chairman Alan Duncan said was “anxiously awaited,” […]
text:
This week the State Board of Education released a new report that detailed $18 billion in school facility needs over the next five years for the state’s 115 school systems. (Image: Adobe Stock)North Carolina is seeing a steep jump in what it needs to spend on its public school facilities, according to a new report by the state Department of Public Instruction. A newly passed constitutional amendment could make that more difficult.  
The 2025–26 statewide facility needs survey, which Vice Chairman Alan Duncan said was “anxiously awaited,” outlined nearly $18 billion in projected public school facility needs across North Carolina over the next five years — a 37% increase from the state’s previous survey in 2020–21.
The assessment, conducted every five years, gives state education officials a snapshot of upcoming construction and renovation projects, while establishing a baseline to track how capital demands have grown across all 115 school districts.
Beyond the five-year window, the survey estimates another $14.78 billion in facility needs for years six through 10, bringing total projected needs over the decade to nearly $33 billion.
“Where is the money going to come from?” Duncan asked during the board meeting. 
The report estimates that districts will need roughly $6.2 billion to construct new schools. Inflation has driven up construction costs, with baseline costs for new school construction reaching $350 per square foot in the latest assessment, up from $250 in 2020–21. The $350 figure does not cover furniture, technology, or equipment. 
However, the larger share of projected spending is for renovations, rather than new construction. The report estimates renovation needs will cost  nearly $9.8 billion, a 77% increase from the previous survey. “More renovations-focused is what we’re seeing in the survey,” said Nathan Maune, director of the Department of Public Instruction’s Office of School Facilities, who presented the report’s findings to the board Wednesday. 
North Carolina seeks $40 million to help schools cover rising fuel costs

Local districts reported plans for renovation projects at more than 1,400 schools across 93 of North Carolina’s 115 school systems. Deferred maintenance and repairs, building code and life-safety upgrades, and HVAC improvements accounted for about 80% of all planned work, according to the presentation. 
School districts currently operate more than 6,200 buildings across 2,451 schools. Roughly 67% of those facilities are more than 30 years old, while 29% are more than 60 years old.
The massive renovation estimate prompted Duncan to question whether state and local officials should reassess how they fund work on older buildings. 
“We don’t do this as a state, but you need to take a step back and look at, are renovations really making sense?” he said. “If it’s going up at a 76% rate, and we’re putting $9 billion in renovation and less than that in new schools, that’s a fair question to ask.” 
Funding for these projects relied on a mix of state and local sources over the past five fiscal years. The state provided roughly $2.83 billion through three lottery-funded capital programs between fiscal years 2021–22 and 2025–26, while voters in eight counties authorized $5.88 billion in local school bonds. 
Most of North Carolina’s 100 counties, however, have not passed school construction bonds, leaving rural and lower-wealth districts with limited ways to raise capital locally, Duncan noted. 
He raised concerns over whether a constitutional amendment approved by voters this week could restrict local government property tax revenue typically tapped for school bonds, though the exact financial impacts of the amendment will depend on how lawmakers implement the measure. 
“I think this report highlights, in many ways, the crossroads we find ourselves at,” Duncan said. “And how we respond to that will speak volumes about what we’re saying about the future of our children in this state.”

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming voters dodged a big-time bullet by defeating Prop 1
description:
If the state had approved a 50% residential property tax cut, it would suffer a major loss of essential services, columnist Kerry Drake opines.
The post Wyoming voters dodged a big-time bullet by defeating Prop 1 appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming didn’t catch any part of that mighty blue wave that washed over much of the country in Tuesday’s midterm election, but I don’t think anyone seriously thought it would.

Opinion

It did, however, dodge a major bullet by rejecting a dud of an idea that would have resulted in major cuts to essential services throughout the state. Wyoming communities could not have absorbed that much pain.
The Equality State did what it’s done in most elections for years: send an all-Republican congressional delegation back to Washington, D.C., elect a slate of GOP state officeholders and put Republican supermajorities in both houses of the Legislature.
But in one vital nonpartisan area, Wyoming voters came together and scored a smashing victory over an attempt to cut most residential property taxes by a whopping 50%.
If the Proposition 1 initiative had passed Tuesday, opponents said Wyoming could have lost $125 million a year or more in property tax revenue, resulting in major cuts to essential services, including law enforcement, fire protection, emergency medical services, hospitals, schools, roads and bridges.
And that revenue would have just disappeared; the initiative didn’t provide any means to replace it. During previous legislative discussions about either cutting property taxes by 50% or eliminating them altogether, some lawmakers had proposed increasing the state sales tax to “backfill” the lost revenue.
Fortunately, Prop 1 failed. According to unofficial final results, 58% of voters opposed or didn’t vote on Prop 1, while a total of 42% backed the measure. If a voter left the question blank, it was counted as a “no” vote.
This misguided idea was the brainchild of three people: Brent Bien, who was endorsed by the Wyoming Republican Party but finished third in this year’s GOP gubernatorial primary; his former campaign manager, Rich Weber, and ex-Wyoming Republican Party state committeewoman Cheryl Aguiar.



Two years ago this trio began a movement to get the massive tax exemption on the ballot for the 2024 election. While they failed to collect enough signatures to make the deadline, Secretary of State Chuck Gray certified the initiative for 2026 after his office verified more than 30,000 signatures of registered voters in January 2025.
It was a stunning accomplishment, the first citizen’s initiative to be placed on a Wyoming ballot in 30 years. One of the reasons for the extreme dry spell is because the state has such a high bar for ballot initiatives, which must obtain signatures equal to 15% of the votes cast in the previous general election’s U.S. House race.
Moreover, the signatures must come from registered voters in at least two-thirds of the state’s 23 counties, which is 16 counties.
The Legislature has rejected attempts to lower the bar, obviously because lawmakers want to make the laws, and not turn that power directly over to voters. 
In the case of the long-winded “People’s Initiative to Limit Property Tax in Wyoming Through a Homeowner’s Property Exemption,” it initially appeared to many political observers as one issue that had a great chance of passing.
Within a few months after its ballot certification, I heard of — but did not specifically see — polling data that found more than 80% of the state’s likely voters viewed the initiative favorably. I didn’t doubt it.
For people who understood what a dangerous impact such action could have on property tax revenue that goes directly to local governments, special districts and public schools, it appeared potentially devastating.
One of the reasons is because lawmakers in the far-right Freedom Caucus had seemingly convinced the public that passing tax cuts was imperative due to major tax increases that had swept through much of the state.
As home values rose, residential property taxes during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2022 increased by an average of 16%, compared to prior years when annual hikes were 3% to 4%. During the same time of double-digit property tax increases throughout the state, Teton County — the wealthiest county in the nation — saw a 36% increase due to skyrocketing house values.
Some Freedom Caucus members in the House and their Senate allies claimed some homeowners would lose their property unless the Legislature provided some so-called “tax relief.” They made this claim without producing any real-life examples of anyone that would happen to, but the narrative was quickly ingrained by politicians and their constituents as gospel.
In the 2024 election, the Freedom Caucus saw enough members elected to take control of the House. The leadership immediately went to work on bills to cut residential property taxes.
One new law capped the annual increase at 4%. A tax rebate program was expanded. For homeowners of more than 25 years, a temporary 25% tax cut was passed, then made permanent.
These measures had started to work. At the same time, the rapid increases in home values began to subside. Meanwhile, the Freedom Caucus had clearly lost the support of voters in the Aug. 18 Republican primary, as it was booted out of House control and its much-ballyhooed attempt to take over the Senate fizzled.
The cries for property tax cuts died too. Two months before Tuesday’s general election, the Joint Revenue Committee said no to a proposed bill to eliminate residential property taxes that it had approved the previous year. In 2025, the bill died when the House ran out of time to consider it.
The panel’s decision came amid the release of new data showing that the majority of Wyoming homeowners did not take advantage of the 25% property tax cut that the Legislature had approved without any income restrictions.
Clearly, the ballot initiative would have only paved the way for the rich to get richer, while people who owned modest homes would receive a small tax cut.
People had stopped coming to legislative committee meetings demanding that property taxes be cut. During the Joint Revenue Committee’s meeting on sponsoring a bill to let voters amend the Wyoming Constitution by eliminating residential property taxes and a companion measure to backfill it with higher sales taxes, no one spoke for or against the measure.
That particularly pleased Rep. Liz Storer, D-Jackson, who asked the panel, “What is the purpose of these bills, and why would we take the time to continue to move them forward, also given that I do not think they will be met with success in the next Legislature? So help me understand your reasoning.”
No one could.

description: Transportation spending for school districts has nearly doubled this school year as diesel prices have reached record highs. text:
North Carolina school buses are ready to roll out for the start of the 2025-26 school year. (Photo: NCDPI) Transportation spending for school districts has nearly doubled this school year as diesel prices have reached record highs. Now, the North Carolina Department of Public Instruction is asking lawmakers for a one-time $40 million fund to help districts cover the additional costs.
Between August and the beginning of October, school districts in the state spent $17.1 million on 3.8 million gallons of diesel fuel. That’s nearly double the $8.6 million they spent for 3.6 million gallons during the same period last school year, according to data DPI presented to the State Board of Education on Wednesday. Districts also spent $8.6 million on 3.7 million gallons during the same period in the 2024-25 school year.
“We were seeing that school districts are spending about twice as much on fuel in the first couple of months of the school year as they were in the previous two school years, even though they bought the same amount of gallons,” Geoff Coltrane, DPI’s senior director of government affairs and strategy, told board members. 
The money would help districts cover fuel costs above the roughly $3 per gallon included in their transportation funding allocation. It would be distributed to school districts and charter schools based on need, Coltrane said.
Diesel prices in North Carolina hit a record average of more than $6 per gallon earlier this fall, putting so much pressure on school transportation budgets that some district leaders said they may be forced to make cuts elsewhere or use money from their reserves.
NC Gov Stein signs gas tax holiday into law

Last month, the General Assembly suspended the state’s motor fuel tax, including the tax on diesel, through Nov. 30. But the suspension doesn’t help school districts because they’re already exempt from fuel taxes.
The department has already begun sharing the request with lawmakers and legislative staff, Coltrane said. DPI did not provide an estimate of how much individual districts could receive.
Democrats won control of the state House in Tuesday’s midterm elections for the first time since 2010, while Republicans retained a narrow majority in the Senate.
The proposal was part of a broader package of budget priorities DPI presented to the State Board of Education. The department plans to submit its recommendations to the state budget office by early January for consideration in the governor’s budget.
Among the other requests, DPI is seeking $300 million in each year of the two-year budget to help school districts buy new literacy and math instructional materials aligned with recently adopted standards. The department is also asking for $115 million to help districts replace student devices, after a report found that many districts don’t have enough money to replace them.
DPI is also seeking $117 million to increase funding for needs-based school construction grants, and another $25 million for school repairs and renovations. The department wants to increase funding for school health personnel by 20%, which it estimates could help districts hire about 700 additional counselors, nurses, social workers and psychologists.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: School meals focus shifts to North Dakota Legislature after Measure 2 defeat
description: An attempt to guarantee free school meals to K-12 students narrowly failed at the ballot box Tuesday, but the issue isn’t going away in North Dakota.  Supporters and opponents of Measure 2, the defeated constitutional amendment, are looking ahead to next steps. Nearly 51% of voters rejected the measure, while about 49% supported it, according […]
text:
Students eat lunch at Roosevelt Elementary School in Bismarck on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)An attempt to guarantee free school meals to K-12 students narrowly failed at the ballot box Tuesday, but the issue isn’t going away in North Dakota. 
Supporters and opponents of Measure 2, the defeated constitutional amendment, are looking ahead to next steps. Nearly 51% of voters rejected the measure, while about 49% supported it, according to complete but unofficial results.
Sen. Paul Thomas, R-Velva, said Wednesday he thinks there is unanimous support in the state for the core principle of ensuring no child goes hungry. 
“Nobody in North Dakota feels or has any belief that a child should ever not be fed,” said Thomas, who opposed the initiated measure but supports legislative action. “This really isn’t a partisan Republican-Democrat divided issue.”
Voters defeat free school meal ballot measure in North Dakota

An advocate for free school meals in the Legislature said she plans to introduce legislation in 2027 to accomplish what Measure 2 failed to do. 
Rep. LaurieBeth Hager, D-Fargo, the sponsor of a free school meals bill that failed to advance in 2025, said she plans to introduce similar legislation again to require all K-12 schools to offer breakfast and lunch to students at no cost. 
“It’s equalizing the kids. We don’t charge them differently for books. We don’t charge them differently for using the buses,” Hager said. “It’s part of the school day and part of the learning experience.”
Hager said she believes the fact that Measure 2 was a constitutional amendment likely scared off voters who are otherwise supportive of providing free school meals to K-12 students.
“If the powers that be think this needs to be in statute instead of in the constitution, then we will get it done that way,” Hager said. “The fight continues.”
Opponents of the measure, including Gov. Kelly Armstrong, criticized putting school meals in the constitution. The program was estimated to cost $124.3 million to $134.3 million every two years starting in 2027-29. Critics said mandating that spending in the constitution would tie lawmakers’ hands during lean budget years.
Armstrong said Wednesday he doesn’t anticipate a large push by Republican lawmakers to revisit a universal school meals program.
“I just think it’s a little harder politically today than it would have been even six months ago,” he said.
Rep. Mike Nathe, R-Bismarck, said voters rejected Measure 2, and he questioned why state lawmakers would consider going against the voters’ wishes.
“The people of North Dakota spoke. They rejected Measure 2, and we have to respect that,” Nathe said. “But that does not mean we can’t work around the edges a little bit and kind of make some things better.”
Nathe sponsored a school meal bill in the January special session that aimed to head off a constitutional ballot measure. House lawmakers approved the bill, but it lost in the Senate by two votes.
Thomas said he does not support a statutory free school meals bill like Hager’s proposal, but the senator said the election result shows voters expect lawmakers will continue working on the issue.
“They want us to continue working on some of the shortcomings of current policy,” Thomas said.
Thomas is working on policy ideas he plans to introduce in the legislative session that begins in January. His bill is being drafted and he plans to gauge his colleagues’ interest when the Legislative Management committee meets next week. 
Other lawmakers, including Rep. Chuck Walen, R-New Town, have said they plan to propose alternative solutions on school meals. Sen. Michelle Axtman, R-Bismarck, said the issue has not been “put to bed,” and expects to make progress during the session.
“I think we’ll find a way to maximize federal dollars and be very strategic and problem-solving to come up with a solution that makes more sense than the measure did,” Axtman said in an interview Tuesday night.
North Dakota families can face debt collections if they can’t afford school lunch

While North Dakota lawmakers have voted against free school meal bills, they have adopted other proposals including an anti-lunch shaming bill in 2023. However, more than two dozen school districts reported in a survey that they refer families to collection agencies for unpaid lunch debt.
Legislators also have slightly expanded how many students qualify for free and reduced lunch through the federal program. In 2025, lawmakers earmarked $6 million to raise the income level used to determine families’ eligibility. 
About $2.5 million of that funding was spent in the first half of the 2025-27 budget cycle, said Lynelle Johnson, director of the Office of Child Nutrition and Food Distribution for the North Dakota Department of Public Instruction. The funding has helped about 3,000 students who would not have otherwise qualified under the federal free and reduced lunch income eligibility requirements. 
“That additional expanded eligibility is very appreciated,” Johnson said.
Robin Nelson, chair of Together for School Meals, said many North Dakotans gave their “time, energy and heart” to the Measure 2 campaign because they saw a need in their schools and communities. 
“We wish we could have given North Dakota families better news. They are why we took on this effort, and they remain our concern as we consider what comes next,” Nelson said. 
Amy Jacobson, the group’s spokesperson, said members of the coalition are going to take time to digest the results and consult with stakeholders before they make any decisions on what they will focus on moving forward. 
“Families are still stretching their budgets, and children still need meals to get through the school day ready to learn,” Jacobson said.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com. Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: Virginia voters split on 1% sales tax for school construction
description: On Election Day, out of 47 Virginia localities, about 30% authorized their governments to collect a 1% sales tax to address rising school construction costs, while about 70% did not.  In June, state lawmakers authorized localities, pending voter support, to raise revenue for school construction and modernization with a 1% sales tax. text:
An early view of the school construction work in Halifax County. (Photo courtesy of Halifax County Public Schools)On Election Day, out of 47 Virginia localities, about 30% authorized their governments to collect a 1% sales tax to address rising school construction costs, while about 70% did not. 
In June, state lawmakers authorized localities, pending voter support, to raise revenue for school construction and modernization with a 1% sales tax. The state estimates over 1000 school buildings are more than 50 years old, and would take $25 billion to rebuild or improve. 
House Education Committee Chair Sam Rasoul, D-Roanoke, and Sen. Jeremy McPike, D-Prince William, proposed the idea last January. Both measures were ultimately added to the state’s budget.
“School construction is a critical need,” said McPike ahead of the results. “This is a direct question to the voters in the form of a referendum, and it’s up to the voters to decide how they want to fund school construction.”
Tuesday’s results are expected to help 14 localities move the needle on school modernization, while leaving questions about the 33 that rejected the opportunity and what comes next.

Rasoul said the idea was to help address billions in school construction needs in the commonwealth. But citizens have raised concerns about tax increases, a point former Gov. Glenn Youngkin raised in previous years
Mecklenburg, one of the nine localities with state-approved authority, has not put the matter to voters since receiving authorization, largely because it opposed raising taxes, according to Board of Supervisors’ records in 2021. 
Mecklenburg estimated it would need about $6 million per year in debt payments to move forward with new school construction, which ultimately dampened interest in adding the option to ballots. 
In addition, the county had already invested in newer additions to the three elementary schools. 
No action has been taken since former state Sen. Frank Ruff successfully proposed the change in 2020.
In 2019, Halifax County became the first locality to receive authority from the state, which is required since Virginia is a “Dillon’s Rule” state, meaning local governments can only exercise powers granted by the state legislature. 
Localities can adjust property tax rates, but they need General Assembly approval to change sales taxes.
With the election’s results, the list has grown from the original nine — city of Danville and the counties of Charlotte, Gloucester, Halifax, Henry, Mecklenburg, Northampton, Patrick and Pittsylvania — to 23 locations.
Rasoul acknowledged that, while he championed the bill, it is not a long-term solution to the state’s school construction needs. Additional support, particularly at the state level, will be necessary to help struggling school divisions, he said.
“This isn’t going to be able to build all the schools that need to be built,” Rasoul said. “So there’s a lot more that needs to be done … even at the state level to help struggling school divisions.”
McPike said upcoming discussions with his colleagues on the Commission on School Construction and Modernization should focus on analyzing the referendum results once they are available, evaluating long-term funding structures for school construction and reviewing stabilized projections over time.
The commission and all state lawmakers will return to Richmond on Jan. 13, 2027 to discuss future legislation and budget amendments.
